title: A mountain humbled
hook: had We sent this Qur'an on a mountain, you'd see it humbled and split (59:21)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghad, and your line was what have I sent ahead? What did you send on today? Day six hundred twenty.

A mountain doesn't move. You can lean your whole weight against one and it won't notice. It was there before every person you know was born, and it'll be there after. Weather breaks on it. Centuries go past it. Nothing about it seems to need anything. It's hard to imagine anything that could make a mountain tremble. Surah Al-Hashr, in its closing verses, imagines exactly that. And what it imagines shaking the mountain isn't an earthquake. It's a book.

Verse twenty-one. Pickthall: "If We had caused this Qur'an to descend upon a mountain, thou (O Muhammad) verily hadst seen it humbled, rent asunder by the fear of Allah." Two words carry the picture. Khashi'an, humbled, from the same root as khushu', the stillness of prayer we met a week ago. And mutasaddi'an, split, cracking apart. The mountain bows, and then it breaks. Then the verse explains itself: such parables we strike for people, so that they may reflect. It's a comparison, and the point lands on us. If the weight of this speech would humble a mountain, what is it doing to a human heart that hears it and stays the same? The Qur'an has shown a mountain like this before. In Surah Al-A'raf, Musa asks to see God. He's told to look at the mountain: if it stays in place, you will see me. And when his Lord revealed himself to the mountain, it crumbled to dust, and Musa fell down senseless. And in Surah Al-Ahzab, God offers the trust to the heavens, the earth and the mountains. They decline it, afraid of it, and the human being takes it on. So the mountains in the Qur'an know their limits. The startling part is the reversal. The hardest thing in the landscape trembles, while a person can listen to the same words and feel nothing. The verse doesn't scold. It holds up the mountain like a mirror and leaves its hearers to reflect.

segments.voice: The practice: stand before a hill. If you can see a hill, a tall building or even a big tree, stand and face it. If not, close your eyes and picture the largest mountain you've ever seen. Stand tall, feet planted. Breathe. Feel how solid you are, and how solid it is. Then, if you pray, let your shoulders soften a little, as a sign of humility before what's greater. If not, simply notice what it's like to be small next to something vast. The bell holds the time.
Musa: the prophet who asked to see God, after which the mountain he stood by crumbled to dust, a mountain's trembling named again in Surah Al-Hashr. Today's word.
Your line: the mountain would crumble. Today, read or hear one verse, or one line that matters to you, slowly, and let it move something. Day six hundred twenty.

howItsDone: The last verses of Surah Al-Hashr, from this verse to the end, are often recited together, and many Muslims read 59:21 as a call to let the Qur'an soften the heart.

fork.setup: you're Musa, asking to see God. you're told: look at the mountain; if it stays in its place, you'll see me. what happens?
options: the mountain stands, and Musa sees.
the mountain crumbles to dust, and Musa falls senseless.
fork.reveal: the mountain crumbled, and Musa fell down. Al-Hashr's mountain, humbled by the Qur'an, echoes that scene.

original.note: Arabic: humbled, split apart. khashi'an shares a root with khushu', the stillness of prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dramatic image of the Qur'an's power.
what it means: a parable that turns into a mirror: the mountain would tremble; what about you?
what a scholar hears: 'tilka l-amthalu nadribuha' marks it as a mathal; read with 7:143 (Musa and the mountain) and 33:72 (the trust declined by the mountains).
